title: Plant Responses to the Environment
seo_title: Grade 12 Life Sciences: Plant Responses to the Environment Worksheets (CAPS)
standard_code: Grade 12 Life Sciences: Responding to the environment: plants
standard_text: Plant hormones: auxins, gibberellins and abscisic acid and their functions; phototropism and geotropism; apical dominance; uses of plant hormones in agriculture; plant defence mechanisms: physical and chemical defences. (summary of CAPS Life Sciences, Grade 12, Life Sciences: Responding to the environment: plants)
meta_desc: Free Grade 12 Life Sciences worksheets (CAPS): auxins, gibberellins, abscisic acid, phototropism, geotropism, apical dominance and plant defences. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Auxin moves to the shaded side of a shoot.
key_sub: Shoots grow towards light; roots grow towards gravity.
body_html:
How to think about it

Plants respond to stimuli by growth movements called tropisms. Phototropism: auxin collects on the shaded side of a shoot, where cells grow longer, so the shoot bends towards the light. Geotropism: roots grow downwards (positive) and shoots upwards (negative). The shoot tip makes auxin that inhibits side buds (apical dominance).

Gibberellins stimulate germination, stem elongation and fruit growth; abscisic acid closes stomata and keeps seeds dormant. Auxins are used as rooting powders and weedkillers. Plants defend themselves physically (thorns, hairs, thick bark) and chemically (bitter tannins and poisons).

Example

A seedling is lit from the left. Which way does it bend?

Towards light

Answer: to the left

Example

Which hormone closes stomata in a drought?

Stress hormone

Answer: abscisic acid

Common mistakes

  • Thinking auxin collects on the lit side.
  • Thinking roots grow away from gravity.
  • Thinking plants cannot defend themselves.

faq.q: Why does pruning the tip make a plant bushier?
faq.a: It removes apical dominance, so the side buds grow into branches.

faq.q: How do acacias defend themselves against browsers?
faq.a: With thorns and by making more bitter tannins in their leaves.

items.q: Which hormone causes phototropism?
items.e: Auxin moves to the shaded side of the shoot.

items.q: Shoots grow upwards, away from gravity. This is …
items.e: Shoots grow against gravity.

items.q: A seedling is placed on a slowly turning clinostat in the dark. How does it grow?
c: straight, because gravity acts on all sides equally
items.e: The clinostat cancels the effect of one-sided gravity.

items.q: In roots, a high concentration of auxin …
c: slows growth, so the root bends downwards
items.e: Roots are more sensitive to auxin than shoots.

items.q: Where is auxin made in a shoot?
c: in the growing tip (apex) of the shoot
items.e: It moves down from the tip to the region of elongation.

items.q: Light shines on a shoot from the left. Where does auxin collect?
items.e: Auxin moves away from the light.

items.q: Roots grow downwards. This is …
items.e: Roots grow in the direction of gravity.

items.q: A shoot tip is cut off and the shoot is lit from one side. What happens?
c: it bends away from the light
it does not bend, because the source of auxin is removed
it bends sharply towards the light
items.e: Without the tip there is no auxin to move.

items.q: A shoot grows towards light. This is …
items.e: Phototropism is a response to light.

items.q: A seedling is placed on its side. After a few days the root bends down and the shoot up. Why?
c: auxin collects on the lower side; it speeds up shoot growth but slows root growth
the seedling was watered from above
auxin collects on the upper side
items.e: Gravity makes auxin move to the lower side.

items.q: What is the stimulus in geotropism?
items.e: Geo- means earth.

items.q: What is the stimulus in phototropism?
items.e: Photo- means light.

items.q: In an experiment on phototropism, what is the control?
c: a seedling in the dark only, with no other plants
an identical seedling with light from all sides (or from above)
items.e: The control is the same but without one-sided light.

items.q: Tendrils of a pea plant coil around a stick. This response to touch is called …
items.e: Tendrils respond to contact.

items.q: Why is it useful for roots to show positive geotropism?
c: they grow down into the soil to anchor the plant and find water
items.e: Roots need water and minerals and must anchor the plant.

items.q: A shoot tip is covered with a foil cap and lit from one side. What happens?
c: the shoot grows straight up and does not bend
it bends away from the light
items.e: The tip detects the light; covered, it cannot respond.

items.q: What is a tropism?
c: the closing of flowers at night
a quick movement of an animal
a growth movement of a plant in response to a stimulus from one direction
items.e: Plants grow towards or away from the stimulus.

items.q: What does auxin do to cells in a shoot?
c: it stops them from dividing forever
items.e: More auxin on one side makes that side grow faster.

items.q: Why does a shoot bend towards light?
c: cells on the lit side grow faster
cells on the shaded side elongate more because of more auxin
the shoot shrinks on the shaded side
items.e: Uneven growth bends the shoot.

items.q: A seedling in a box with one hole grows towards the hole. Which factor is tested?
items.e: The shoot grows towards the light coming in.

items.q: What is the sigmoid growth curve?
c: an S-shaped curve with lag, log (exponential) and stationary phases
items.e: Seen in cells, tissues and organs.

items.q: Which effect is caused by cytokinin?
c: stem elongation and bolting in cabbage
apical dominance and root initiation on stem cuttings
cell division and delaying leaf senescence
items.e: Cytokinin: cell division and delaying leaf senescence.

items.q: Which plant hormone causes stem elongation and bolting in cabbage?
items.e: Gibberellin: stem elongation and bolting in cabbage.

items.q: Which hormone causes bolting in cabbage?
items.e: Bolting is rapid stem growth before flowering.

items.q: Why is abscisic acid called a stress hormone?
c: it makes the plant grow fast
it is made when the plant is short of water and closes the stomata
items.e: It helps the plant survive drought.

items.q: Which plant hormone causes cell division and delaying leaf senescence?
items.e: Cytokinin: cell division and delaying leaf senescence.

items.q: Which plant hormone causes apical dominance and root initiation on stem cuttings?
items.e: Auxin: apical dominance and root initiation on stem cuttings.

items.q: Which effect is caused by gibberellin?
c: closing stomata and seed dormancy (the stress hormone)
cell division and delaying leaf senescence
apical dominance and root initiation on stem cuttings
stem elongation and bolting in cabbage
items.e: Gibberellin: stem elongation and bolting in cabbage.

items.q: Rooting powder is used on cuttings. Which hormone does it contain?
items.e: Auxin stimulates roots to form.

items.q: Why do selective weedkillers kill broad-leaved weeds but not grass?
c: broad leaves absorb more synthetic auxin, which makes them grow out of control and die
items.e: The weeds grow too fast and die.

items.q: Name a plant hormone that ripens fruit.
items.e: Ethylene gas speeds up ripening; one ripe banana ripens others nearby.

items.q: What is apical dominance?
c: the growing shoot tip stops lateral buds from growing
items.e: Removing the tip (as in tea plants) gives a bushy plant.

items.q: Which plant hormone causes fruit ripening and leaf fall?
items.e: Ethylene: fruit ripening and leaf fall.

items.q: What is the difference between a plant hormone and an animal hormone?
c: animal hormones only act in plants
plant hormones are made in many tissues and often act nearby; animal hormones come from glands and travel in the blood
items.e: Plants have no endocrine glands.

items.q: Which effect is caused by abscisic acid?
c: stem elongation and bolting in cabbage
closing stomata and seed dormancy (the stress hormone)
apical dominance and root initiation on stem cuttings
items.e: Abscisic acid: closing stomata and seed dormancy (the stress hormone).

items.q: Which hormone helps barley seeds produce enzymes when they germinate?
items.e: Gibberellin makes the aleurone layer release amylase.

items.q: Which hormone is called the stress hormone?
items.e: It helps plants survive drought.

items.q: Which hormone inhibits the growth of side buds?
items.e: This is apical dominance.

items.q: Which hormone is found in coconut milk and maize kernels?
items.e: Kinetin was first found in autoclaved herring sperm DNA.

items.q: Why are unripe fruits sometimes stored with a ripe banana?
c: the banana gives off ethene, which speeds up ripening
items.e: Ethylene is a gaseous plant hormone.

items.q: How are gibberellins used in agriculture?
c: to produce larger, seedless grapes and to malt barley
items.e: They increase fruit size and speed up germination.

items.q: What is the arithmetic growth equation?
items.e: Only one daughter cell keeps dividing.

items.q: A gardener cuts the top off a plant to make it bushy. Why does this work?
c: removing the tip removes the source of auxin, so side buds grow
items.e: This removes apical dominance.

items.q: Which effect is caused by auxin?
c: apical dominance and root initiation on stem cuttings
cell division and delaying leaf senescence
closing stomata and seed dormancy (the stress hormone)
stem elongation and bolting in cabbage
items.e: Auxin: apical dominance and root initiation on stem cuttings.

items.q: What is NAA used for in agriculture?
c: hastening fruit ripening and flowering in pineapple
increasing the length of grape stalks and sugarcane stems
items.e: NAA: rooting of stem cuttings.

items.q: What is ethephon used for in agriculture?
c: hastening fruit ripening and flowering in pineapple
increasing the length of grape stalks and sugarcane stems
items.e: Ethephon: hastening fruit ripening and flowering in pineapple.

items.q: What is dedifferentiation?
c: differentiated cells regaining the ability to divide
items.e: e.g. formation of cork cambium from parenchyma.

items.q: Which hormone keeps seeds and buds dormant?
items.e: It prevents germination at the wrong time.

items.q: What is photoperiodism?
c: the response of plants to the relative lengths of day and night
items.e: It controls flowering.

items.q: Which chemical is used for increasing the length of grape stalks and sugarcane stems?
items.e: GA₃: increasing the length of grape stalks and sugarcane stems.

items.q: What is vernalisation?
c: promotion of flowering by a period of low temperature
items.e: e.g. winter wheat and biennials.

items.q: Which hormone stimulates seed germination and stem elongation?
items.e: Gibberellins break dormancy and make stems longer.

items.q: Which hormone causes stomata to close in dry conditions?
items.e: It reduces water loss during drought.

items.q: What is GA₃ used for in agriculture?
c: increasing the length of grape stalks and sugarcane stems
hastening fruit ripening and flowering in pineapple
items.e: GA₃: increasing the length of grape stalks and sugarcane stems.

items.q: Which chemical is used for hastening fruit ripening and flowering in pineapple?
items.e: Ethephon: hastening fruit ripening and flowering in pineapple.

items.q: How are auxins used in agriculture?
c: as weedkillers and rooting powder for cuttings
items.e: Synthetic auxins kill broad-leaved weeds and help cuttings grow roots.

items.q: Which effect is caused by ethene?
c: apical dominance and root initiation on stem cuttings
closing stomata and seed dormancy (the stress hormone)
cell division and delaying leaf senescence
items.e: Ethylene: fruit ripening and leaf fall.

items.q: What is heterophylly?
c: the same leaf in all plants
different shapes of leaves on the same plant
items.e: e.g. buttercup in water and in air.

items.q: What is apical dominance?
c: side buds grow faster than the tip
the main shoot tip makes auxin that stops side buds from growing
items.e: Removing the tip lets side branches grow.

items.q: Which chemical is used for killing broad-leaved weeds?
items.e: 2,4-D: killing broad-leaved weeds.

items.q: How do enzymes speed up reactions?
items.e: They provide an alternative route.

items.q: What is a limiting factor in photosynthesis?
c: the factor in shortest supply that limits the rate
a factor that has no effect
items.e: Light intensity, CO₂ concentration and temperature.

items.q: Why does the rate of photosynthesis fall at very high temperatures?
c: enzymes such as rubisco are denatured
items.e: Stomata may also close.

items.q: What is the advantage of positive phototropism?
c: leaves get more light for photosynthesis
items.e: More light means more food.

items.q: Why do seeds of some fynbos plants germinate only after a fire?
c: fire kills all insects for ever
the seeds need the heat to photosynthesise
chemicals in the smoke break their dormancy, so they grow when there is less competition
fire adds water to the soil
items.e: Smoke-stimulated germination is an adaptation to fire.

items.q: A starch solution takes 160 s to be broken down by amylase. Calculate the rate as 1/time.
Why do growers burn paraffin in greenhouses?
c: it raises CO₂ concentration and temperature
items.e: Both can limit photosynthesis.

items.q: In a phototropism investigation, which is the independent variable?
c: the time of day the results are recorded
items.e: The investigator changes the direction of light and observes the response.

items.q: Which factor must be kept the same in a phototropism investigation?
c: the type of seedling, water and temperature
items.e: Controlled variables keep the test fair.

items.q: In a chromatogram of leaf pigments, a pigment spot moves 5,4 cm and the solvent moves 9,0 cm. Calculate its R<sub>f</sub> value.
How does a non-competitive inhibitor work?
c: it binds to the active site
it raises the activation energy only
it binds away from the active site and changes its shape
items.e: More substrate does not reduce its effect.

items.q: What happens to a shoot if auxin is placed on its left side only?
items.e: The left side grows faster, so the shoot bends away from that side.

items.q: Where does the Calvin cycle (light-independent reaction) take place?
items.e: It uses ATP and reduced NADP.

items.q: Why are tropism experiments with roots often done in the dark?
c: auxin is destroyed in the dark
to make sure the response is to gravity and not to light
roots grow faster in the dark only
items.e: Removing light removes a second stimulus.

items.q: Why are many seedlings used in a tropism investigation, not just one?
c: to make the seedlings grow faster
to make the results more reliable
so that the experiment is quicker
items.e: Repeating reduces the effect of chance differences.

items.q: Which describes the growth of a pollen tube down the style to the ovule?
items.e: The tube grows towards chemicals from the ovule.

items.q: In a chromatogram of leaf pigments, a pigment spot moves 6,0 cm and the solvent moves 9,0 cm. Calculate its R<sub>f</sub> value.
Why do shoots in the dark grow tall and pale?
c: they use stored food to grow quickly upwards to reach light, and make no chlorophyll
items.e: This is called etiolation.

items.q: Which hormone was first isolated from human urine?
items.e: Auxin means 'to grow'.

items.q: Roots grow towards water in the soil. This is …
items.e: Hydro- means water.

items.q: Some plants make chemicals that attract wasps when caterpillars eat them. Why?
items.e: Plants can 'call for help' from predators of their pests.

items.q: Some plants have stinging hairs. What kind of defence is this?
items.e: Hairs and spines are physical barriers.

items.q: Why do farmers in South Africa plant crops that resist insects?
c: the crops need less pesticide, which is cheaper and better for the environment
the crops do not need sunlight
items.e: Resistant crops have strong natural defences.

items.q: Why do some plants grow sharp thorns only on low branches?
c: the low branches are the ones animals can reach
items.e: Defence is put where it is most needed.

items.q: Why do some acacias produce more tannin when giraffes browse them?
c: tannins make the leaves bitter, so animals eat less
items.e: It is a chemical defence that is switched on by damage.

items.q: What is 2,4-D used for in agriculture?
c: increasing the length of grape stalks and sugarcane stems
hastening fruit ripening and flowering in pineapple
items.e: 2,4-D: killing broad-leaved weeds.

items.q: Which is a chemical defence of a plant?
c: producing nicotine or caffeine that is toxic to insects
items.e: Many such chemicals are used as natural insecticides.

items.q: Which plant has spines instead of leaves to reduce water loss and to defend itself?
items.e: Spines protect it from animals and lose little water.

items.q: Why does a thick bark help a tree?
c: it absorbs water from the air
it protects the tree from insects, fire and drying out
it helps the tree to flower
items.e: Bark is a physical barrier.

items.q: Why do plants need to respond to their environment?
c: so that they can move from place to place
to get enough light, water and nutrients and to protect themselves
items.e: Responses improve survival.

items.q: Which is a chemical defence of a plant?
c: making bitter or poisonous substances such as tannins
items.e: Chemicals make plants unpleasant or toxic to eat.

items.q: What does a thorn on an acacia tree do?
c: it is a physical defence against grazing animals
items.e: Plants defend themselves physically and chemically.

items.q: Why do some plants have a strong smell or bitter taste?
c: the chemicals discourage animals from eating them
items.e: This is a chemical defence.

items.q: Which hormone was discovered from the 'bakanae' disease of rice?
items.e: Gibberella fujikuroi caused tall seedlings.

items.q: Which is a physical defence of a plant?
c: a waxy cuticle and thick cell walls that stop fungi entering
items.e: Physical barriers stop pathogens and insects.

items.q: Where is the stimulus for photoperiodic flowering perceived?
items.e: A hormone then moves to the shoot tip.

items.q: Which defence do grasses have against grazing animals?
c: silica in their leaves, which makes them tough and wears down teeth
items.e: Silica is a physical defence.

items.q: Which plant hormone causes closing stomata and seed dormancy (the stress hormone)?
items.e: Abscisic acid: closing stomata and seed dormancy (the stress hormone).

items.q: Which hormone is a gas?
items.e: It speeds ripening.

items.q: How do some plants defend themselves when they are wounded?
c: they produce chemicals that slow down the growth of fungi and bacteria
items.e: Wounds are entry points for pathogens.
